Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that that was established in the -- or mentioned in 91 document. The previous proposal by General Markac, I may have missed the reference to a particular special police unit, but it was -- I understood the document as being a proposal for the use of special police as such without specified -- specific unit being identified, but maybe I missed it on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In item 2 of the instruction mention is made of the operation commander appointment, stating that he is the person who is supposed to implement and bring forth orders concerning the individual sectors within which the special police forces are to be active. This is another document in the creation of the joint police special police forces. Could I have a document number for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number D1090. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1090 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may we have 3D01-0682.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was also issued by the special police sector commander Mr. Markac, sent to the Minister of the Interior Mr. Jarnjak, and Deputy Minister, Mr. Zeljko Tomljenovic. In the introductory part of the document, which I suppose you did not see, am I correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in the introductory part of the document, mention is made of the commander of the Main Staff of the HV with the agreement of the Minister of Interior of the Republic of Croatia, and pursuant to that agreement this order is being issued by virtue of which the special police department should organise an attack operation in cooperation with the forces of the Croatian army. In the second paragraph it is mentioned that the joint special police forces should group along two major axes of attack in the area of Mount Velebit, and we have specific locations mentioned in the subsequent paragraph such as Vrsine, Mali Alan and Plantaze. If we move to the second page of the document, we see that in this operation under the name of Poskok 5, there is a joint forces staff that is being formed and certain individuals appointed to that staff. Do you agree, Mr. Theunens, that we can see that this was another step in the genesis leading towards the creation of a joint special police forces staff? This document was drafted by Minister of the Interior Ivan Jarnjak with the agreement of Deputy Minister Mr. Tomljenovic, and as we said, they were the people who were supposed to issue the approval on the use of the special forces of the police from individual administrations in order to carry out a joint operation. Do you agree with me concerning that interpretation of mine, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure whether it's -- it's -- I would use the word genesis. It's just an example or another example of, as you stated, the establishment -- no, the preparation of -- of operations to be conducted by special police units whereby an ad hoc command structure is being established in order to command and control the specific operation or action as it is here -- as it is called here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May we have tendered this document into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number D1091, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1091 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you pull up on the screen D534, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were discussing the use of special police in specific circumstances during ad hoc operations when joint forces are formed and when special police is used in actual combat. We are now to turn to a part of the minutes drafted at Brioni on the 17th of July, 1995. It was a meeting of the president of the republic, Dr. Tudjman, with a delegation from the Minister of Defence and senior military officials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the last document, that is the document you said was drafted by the Minister Jarnjak and Mr. Tomljenovic, the original shows a huge black part on the first page. Is there any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have no explanation for that black part. That's the copy that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but apparently it's redacted in one way or another. I don't know where it stems from. Is it an OTP document or is it a document you obtained, because usually if there is no explanation we do not easily accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been advised that this document we obtained from the Ministry of Interior as it is. So I have no explanation for the black mark on the front page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you asked for an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you asked for it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was interested in the substance of the document, not the -- maybe it's not only formality, I agree with you, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be just a stamp or handwriting, whatever, but someone took the effort to make parts of the document invisible. Could you please report to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll do so. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, as I said, this is the minutes of a meeting at Brioni on the 17th of July. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... to go to the page ERN number 01324982. This is page 48 of the document in the printed version. I don't know which is the page in the e-court version. Yes, that's the one. [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, did you have an opportunity to study these minutes from the meeting in Brioni?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I have reviewed these minutes, and I think I have included them but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Let it be like it is. [Interpretation] Please allow me to focus your attention to the part in the second paragraph beginning with the words "General Markac." Although it is not visible from the minutes, but it was part of the address of Dr. Tudjman whereby he said General Markac mentioned the problem of special forces of the interior. I won't take you through the whole text for the sake of time, which is limited. He also says, "We should not establish a special parallel army from the special forces of the Ministry of the Interior." Are you following, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] So they can keep their form for now until the liberation, until the end of the war in Croatia and in Bosnia, and then we will make a final decision. Up until then they should remain as they are and should be assigned tasks as part of the joint operations that they can execute, and I believe they can execute them well. In certain regard, they can do that better than some other units. Mr. Theunens, when we interpret this part of the text can we agree that the president, being also the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, believed that the forces of the special police were to be assigned a particular role for specific tasks rather than creating a parallel armed force from those forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're talking about two very distinct things here. President Tudjman on one -- at first indeed states, I mean, about the special police in general terms that it should not be a separate army or a separate armed force; and here, the second part is that they can be given specific tasks within joint operations. I assume he refers here to operations together with the army, but for me those are two distinct things, two distinct aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Theunens. We are now in a situation when in June 1995 in Croatia there was contemplation about liberating that part of the country which for four years had been under the authority of the forces of the so-called ARSK -- RSK. Preparations were made to that end. I would like to show you D956, a directive issued by General Bobetko that you had an opportunity to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have that on the screen. It is Exhibit D956.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, as you have explained in your testimony, you have explained what the purpose of such a document is, the document being a directive. This directive of the 26th of June, 1995, was signed by the chief of the Main Staff General Janko Bobetko. In the heading an operation is mentioned under the code-name of Oluja, or Storm, 4. Could you please remind us, Mr. Theunens, what was the purpose of such a document from the military strategic point of view? What is the purpose of a directive in -- in only a few words, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a directive a senior level of command explains in general terms a mission that has to be accomplished by the subordinates, and the directive will then be used by the subordinate commands to issue more specific orders as to the accomplishment of the general mission or the -- that has been established by the -- what I call the senior level of command, corps or higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you for your answer. [Interpretation] If we go to page 3 of the directive, item 3 of page 3. We have it in Croatian. Do we have it in English as well? No. The English text will probably contain that on page 4. [In English] Yes. Okay. [Interpretation] I would like to refer to item 3 where the tasks of the military district of Split are specified. It is stated therein that the military district Split is to prepare and launch an attack operation in coordination with the forces of the Ministry of the Interior. They should seize Mali Alan and the dominant features on Mount Velebit. On page 4 of the directive, in the same paragraph, in the Croatian, and I believe it is the right page in English, it is stated that through synchronised attempts of the artillery rocket forces and infantry the enemy should be broken up along the following axis and so on and so forth. I am quoting this because there was some mention of MUP forces. If we go to item 14. In the Croatian it is page 6. We see that all HV units should take care to implement fully the provisions of international law when having contact with the civilian population in the occupied territory. In addition to the military police units various forces of the Ministry of the Interior should be employed as well. It is also stated that the operation will have the code-name of Oluja 4. We said already that the document was sent to the military district Split, as well as to the military district Gospic. If we look at D535 next, we shall see that it is an order by General Janko Bobetko sent to the commander of the special MUP forces, Lieutenant General Mladen Markac. Could we please go to page 2 of the document -- or, rather, let's stay with this page. Well, it doesn't matter. We see the order here sent to General Mladen Markac. On the next page we'll see that it is also forwarded for information to the commanders of the military districts of Gospic and Split. Could you please explain, Mr. Theunens, why the military districts of Gospic and Split were sent this directive from the Main Staff and the commander of the special forces is being sent this order? We see that it is far shorter than the directive itself. Why did the special forces not receive the directive itself? What is your explanation in this situation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I cannot give a clear answer. Normally, a commander or subordinate commander receives only the information from his superior he needs to have in order to carry out his mission. We would have to compare both documents in order to see whether in the directive there's anything included that pertains to the special police which is not included in the order that General Markac has received. If that would be the case, then there is problem. Otherwise, I do not really see anything significant in this distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I agree with that, Mr. Theunens. However, my question was: Why was this done in this manner? Do you have an explanation accounting for that? Is there some sort of military doctrine which can explain why in relation to some commanders the Supreme Command sends them a directive, whereas it sends orders to other commanders?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said -- well, you have to look at the contents of the document. If the order includes all the information that is required for the special police to carry out its -- its mission, in particular also the coordination with the Gospic and the Split Military District, then I don't see any issue in the fact that it's called an order and it's much less complete or comprehensive than the initial directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There is one other fact that surprised me as a layman, and I'd like to hear your comment. Nowhere in this order is the code-name of the operation Oluja mentioned, whereas in the directives addressed to the commanders of the military districts the code-name is mentioned. At page 1 where someone wrote that this was an order for Oluja to General Markac, I don't know who wrote it, but this is evidently not the original part of the document. It was added when it was filed. But you will see that the order itself does not mention Oluja anywhere, whereas the directive does. What is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I cannot give a clear-cut answer, but it may well be that the directive was called Oluja, and that is that this specific order for the special police is a component of the directive whereby, for reasons I ignore, no particular name was given. It's not a must to give a name to an operation. It is often done because it facilitates communication, but I haven't seen anything in the doctrine that states, well, a directive or an order needs to have a name. The most important is the number, because that can be used in order to refer to the -- to the document, number and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you for your question -- answer, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could we see, Mr. Registrar, the document D536.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were able to see that the chief of the Main Staff sent directives to commanders of military districts. We saw that the commander of the special police, General Mladen Markac was given an order. Now we will see a document by Janko Bobetko, chief of the Main Staff, dated the 29th of June, 1995, whereby -- or, rather, which reads that the increased forces of the MUP special units engaged pursuant to his order, and the numbers are listed there, and I tell you that they are identical to the order we saw a moment ago, need to be pulled out to their base immediately. This is in fact an order for retreat, is it not, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I mean the conclusive answer to be given by looking also at the specific order that was given to the special police units, because here you only have one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document we see that it was sent for information to the commanders of the Split and Gospic military districts. Mr. Theunens, studying the general situation at the time, and we're talking about the end of June 1995, having studied that, did you realise that at that time negotiations were being engaged in with the attempt at reaching a peaceful reintegration of the territory that was temporarily occupied by the Serb forces and that the Croatian side was negotiating under the framework of the Z-4 plan, as it was called? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of specific negotiations in the framework of the Z-4 plan at the end of June 1995, but if you refresh my memory that can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We're now coming to the time period of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D549 called up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time for combat purposes, intelligence assessments are made about the strength of the enemy forces in the area of responsibility of the joint forces of the special police in the Velebit area. That's to say the axes we mentioned earlier on, the Mali Alan, the tunnel, and the road leaning from Gospic to Gracac. This is the intelligence assessment submitted by the internal control department, which indicates that in the area of the joint forces of the special police in the Velebit area elements of the 13th Lika Corps were noticed, 9th Motorised Brigade, 7th Knin Corps, and 4th Light Brigade were all found to be present there, that the command post of the brigade was in Gracac and that the forward command post was in the village of Radosevici. The document goes on to speak about the intelligence assessments concerning the strength of the enemy forces. Have you seen this document, Mr. Theunens, while you were drafting your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and it is referred to in footnote 1088 in the second part of the report, page 272.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once the intelligence assessment was made of the strength of the enemy forces which, judging by the figures, was quite a significant one -- let us move on to see document D537. What we have here is the command of the new chief of the Main Staff who replace General Bobetko, and that was General Cervenko. The order is issued in accordance with the directive which, as we were able to see, was issued by the former chief of the Main Staff, General Bobetko. The conclusion I draw from this, and you will correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Theunens, is that the directive issued by General Bobetko had not been withdrawn, whereas the order that General Bobetko issued to General Markac was withdrawn with an order that the forces that were there should retreat to their base. Is this an appropriate analysis on my part?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is indeed possible whereby -- I should have also explained that the directive can -- is actually the basis for orders and a directive can be valid during several weeks or even months because it's like for -- it's the bigger plan. And then smaller plans, to put it in layman's terms, like an order, are being derived from the directive. And even if an earlier order which followed from the directive is withdrawn, there can be a follow-up order or a new order, as we see here with the General Cervenko order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This particular order by General Cervenko requests that 300 special policemen from the area of Zadar, Vir, Knin should be redeployed and given a different assignment, in fact. I should like to call up document D539 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, could you find a suitable moment within the next five minutes for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, what we see is the order by assistant minister sent to the chief of the Brod-Posavina police administration, and it is said that it should be sent to the commander of the special police unit. The order states that he has to provide 120 men with adequate artillery pieces at the disposal of the joint forces of the special police. Can we agree that this document, in fact, indicates that on the basis of General Markac's order joint forces are being set up by elements of the units of police administrations?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is that the order is intended for the special police unit commander, that he is to take 120 members of his unit, and it's not the chief of the Brod-Posavina police administration who is to take these 120 people --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we have completed that topic. I don't intend to go back to it, and I suggest that you do not do that either. So your position is that the chief of the police administration is only the mailbox, as you put it. My position is that the use of the special police units of a given police administration is something that has to be approved by the chief. Our positions are therefore different. Let us not go back to that topic, and Their Honours will judge which of the arguments should be accepted in the proceedings. Another document similar to this one which pulls together policemen from various police administrations can be found, for your reference, in D540, D541, D542, and in document D542 the order was issued by the chief of the special police, Mr. Sacic, who apparently had that particular power. Mr. Theunens, let us go back for a moment to a document we were able to see already and then I will finish for this session. This is D528. I'm referring specifically to page 03549943. This is a list of numbers of members of the various police administrations, that's to say the special police unit members. And I took the time to make my calculations, and I got to the sum of 2.311 active-duty special policemen. The next page shows the number of reserve members of the special police forces, and their number totals at 2.464. The sum total of the special policemen by police administrations is 4.775, the number including both active-duty and reserve members. Mr. Theunens, one other question before the break. Do you know approximately the number of the special police units used during and after Operation Storm, and I mean number of members as part of the joint forces of the special police?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check, Your Honours. It maybe included in part 2 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe this would be a suitable time for the pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you said one other question before the break and that's what you did after doing some arithmetics. I've got no idea what these arithmetics you presented to us are about. I see a document on my screen with a lot of number, and then you say, "I have done my own calculations." Apparently in relation to this, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe I was too quick just in order to save some time, but what I did is a -- I did arithmetic, as you said, and I count all the members of the special police, which is column 1, 2, 3 in that -- in that table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the one starting with 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ending with 287.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is a reserve staff, and the whole number of the column 3 would be 2.464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which means that is the number of the reserve staff of the special police in whole police administration on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, as well as the previous column makes a sum of 2.311, and all together that is 4.775 special policemen from active and reserve staff. This is the number of the special police officers in the Republic of Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still lost. You're adding 2.464 to, you said, the previous column. That's 3.010.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Eleven. It's 2.311. That's the previous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's the previous page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Previous page, right. Because one page is for active staff, and the other page is for reserve staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if someone could make a printout for me so that I do --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's hard to see on the screen, right. We could do the copy, Your Honour, for the Chamber, if you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it an exhibit already?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is. It is Exhibit D528.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have a hard copy, because the problem is that during the breaks I'm logged in here and I can't log in any more at my desk. We will have a break and we will resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the Chamber expects you tomorrow to finish within the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour, and I will finish until the end of the first session. Thank you. May we see the document D539, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've forgotten one thing. The five minutes I promised yesterday will be given at the end, that is on from 20 minutes -- no, as a matter of fact, perhaps it would be wiser to reserve seven or eight minutes so that if anything arises out of the submissions that we have at least a couple of minutes extra.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So could we have document D539, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is very same document that we've seen before, and it's to be seen from the witness. [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We discussed it before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the document, assistant minister Mr. Mladen Markac issued an order to the chief of the Brodsko-Posavska police administration to be forwarded to the commander of the special police unit and that 120 special policemen be dispatched for the purposes of setting up joint forces. So the number is 120. If we go back to the chart we looked at a moment ago, which is D528, then we see that the Brodsko-Posavska special police unit numbers 145 active-duty members and 168 reserve members, the total being 313 members of the special police unit. Since according to this order the Brodsko-Posavska administration was duty-bound to deploy 120 men, 193 remained within the administration. I don't know if you're following me. In other words, not all the members of the special police force were deployed to be part of the joint forces, rather, only a smaller number, the greater part of them remained with the Brodsko-Posavska administration. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just like to reiterate what I said before the break, that it is an order which is from the Assistant Minister of Interior or from the chief of special police sector to the chief of the special police unit in the Brod-Posavina police administration. And yes, indeed, here we have an order for 120 people. There may well have been other orders that are intended to deploy the remaining members of the special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Do you see such order, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from the top of my head, but what I have -- when I reviewed the operations conducted by special police units during and after Operation Storm, we do see, indeed, that components of units or certain members of units are active in one area whereas other components of that unit may be active in another area, together with various components of different special police units. And -- and the -- I must say that the special police documents reviewed were very detailed as to who issued the orders and how many members of which unit were active where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, I showed you the maths in order to demonstrate to you how a number of the special police units remained with their administrations discharging their regular duties, while others were sent to join the joint forces. If we recall the annual analysis of Operation Oluja, some 2.200 members of the special police were reportedly participating in it. Now, the document D598 -- 528 table indicates that the total of 4.775 special police members took part in Operation Storm. My thesis is that only a part of the special police forces took part in Oluja, whereas others stayed behind with their respective administration discharging their usual duties. Do you agree with this case of mine?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether D528, i.e., the table we see now, whether it also allows to draw conclusions as to how many of these -- both active as well as reserve members of the special police did participate in Operation Storm. Maybe there's a separate table which I haven't seen, but this here just shows active-duty staff, and the other page shows reserve staff where it's not clear to what extent, as I said, they participated in Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] I should like to call up document P554. Mr. Theunens, we're about to see a document which you must have looked at. It's a document ordering the setting up and placing into operation a staff of the joint forces of the special police.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and it can be found on English page 297, part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The document says that with a view to ensuring as efficient as possible a command over the joint forces a staff of the joint forces is set up, the person in charge being Colonel -- Colonel-General Mladen Markac. Mr. Theunens, in a situation where Mr. Markac is appointed action commander as part of Operation Storm and in connection with the staff of the joint forces, the rank attached to him is colonel-general. In other documents, in the documents where joint forces are being put together, like D539, Mr. Mladen Markac is signed only in his capacity as assistant minister without the mention of his rank. I'm saying this because we need to distinguish between the function of Mr. Markac in peacetime and his function in combat when the staff of joint forces is being set up. Are you aware of this distinction, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I mean, it's not a direct answer to your question, but I have seen a document, which is 65 ter 5832, which -- and it's referred to in the addendum on page 42, which states that on the 24th of May, 1995, Mladen Markac is promoted to the rank of reserve colonel-general. Now, I have not been able to establish the conditions or the circumstances of this promotion, and I have not been --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm asking you on that promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the question apparently is whether General Markac, appearing in a document as we have in front of us, is referred to by his rank, whereas in many other documents he is referred to in his, if I could say, civilian capacity, civilian position. That's what the question is about. Whether you were aware of this difference and what this difference means to you, that's how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have noted the difference, Your Honour, but I have not been able to draw any particular conclusion from that difference. In any event, in P554, both the rank as well as the civilian title are being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the document before us, and could we please go to page 2 now, we can see in the right-hand side corner we see that Mr. Ivan Jarnjak signed, who was the Minister of the Interior. In keeping with our earlier discussion, then, when the staff was being formed and the joint forces were being formed, the minister's approval is need as well. These cannot be established pursuant to an order of another person. The minister needs to approve that as well. I would kindly ask you to look at the penultimate paragraph of the document which states that the command of the joint forces of the special police is duty-bound to act professionally, in keeping with the Law on the Interior and the various conventions concerning the laws of war. We are getting closer to the date of the beginning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the 65 ter document 1890.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In order to prepare for an operation, certain amount of reconnaissance and intelligence activity is needed in order to establish what the position and number of enemy forces are. Is that correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is part. I mean, intelligence -- we call it intelligence preparation of the battlefield, IPB, is one of the significant activities the operations staff will conduct when planning military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We said earlier that one of the departments of the special police sector was the department in charge of internal control, and it is this document that was authored by Mr. Soljic [phoen], who was the head of that department. He drafted this document on the 29th of July, 1995. In it we see that there is a report on the activities in the area of Mount Velebit, specifying the fortified positions of the enemy, at least according to the intelligence assessment information. We have Tulovegrede referred to, then Mali Alan and so on and so forth. Those were the positions on Mount Velebit that were established as being the fortified positions of the enemy. At page 2 it says that three mixed anti-armour/infantry minefields were located and there is an assessment of axes provided through the enemy defence lines, and these were being suggested by the internal control department as specified in the penultimate paragraph of the second page of the document. One of the axes was Veliki Golic, Opaljenik, Ruje, then Dusica, Veliko Bilo, Bili Kuci, and so on and so forth. In your experience, would this be a customary way of preparing an operation, that is to say to have intelligence assessed to see what the strength of the enemy is and to propose certain axes to carry out an attack?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. It's what I mentioned earlier as IPB, intelligence preparation of the battlefield. And this document can be found in footnote 1088 in part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could this document be marked as in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number D1092. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1092 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could I have, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 2600.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Internal control was in charge of collecting intelligence information and reconnaissance. On the 1st of August, they wrote a new document sent to the Chief of Staff of the joint special police forces specifying that the enemy forces were reinforced in the area of Medak and that they received support in one mortar squad of 120-millimetre in calibre and a number of staff and that in the area of Gracac, during the morning, general mobilisation was being carried out of able-bodied men. It also states that in the area of Korenica, towards the south, there were 19 trucks on the move with personnel as well as certain buses. All this is indicative of a mobilisation and the grouping of forces of the RSK in the area of activity of the special police as envisaged. Did you see this document before, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen the document. It is also included in footnote 1088, and, yes, it gives the -- provides the intelligence available to the internal control department which it shares with the chief of the joint special police staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May this document be marked as in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number D1093. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1093 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar could you please pull up D543.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, we will see an order by General Cervenko, chief of the Main Staff of the HV, dated the 29th of July, sent to Colonel-General Mladen Markac. You are familiar with this document, are you not, Mr. Theunens? The special MUP forces are hereby ordered from their operational base in the area of Mount Velebit to execute attacks along the axes Mali Golic, Sveti Rok, Gracac, Prezid. The tasks are specified: To cut off the Gospic-Gracac road, seize the Celavac radio relay facility, put the pass and the tunnel at Prezid under observation, and link up with the forces of the Split Military District 2nd Battalion and Guards Brigade. I was surprised to find in this document that there is no mention there of Operation Storm. However, you have already provided an explanation stating that it wasn't necessary, although in all of the orders sent to the military districts Operation Storm is referred to. In the document we can read that the operation was to take place in two stages, in the duration of two days. During the first stage we need to seize a particular area. Mr. Theunens, the area referred to is a mountainous area of the Velebit range. It is a very forbidding terrain which is barely inhabited. Can we -- barely populated. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and I'm familiar with the general aspects of the terrain based on my professional activities prior to joining the ICTY, and this document is mentioned or discussed on English page 269 of part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the operation was to comprise two stages. The first stage included a terrain on Velebit, and on page 2 we see the second stage, that is to say introducing the majority of our forces along the axes mentioned, and the seizing of the Celavac radio relay facility. Mr. Theunens, are you familiar with the function, with the role of the radio relay function -- facility of Celavac and its importance for the armed forces of the so-called RSK?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the specifics of the Celavac radio relay station or facility, but I can imagine why such a facility is needed and why also you would like to take control of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Also, I suppose you can comment on why it was important to cut off the road between Gospic and Gracac, which in a way split the territory of the RSK into its northern and southern part. Without any doubt it was a very strategic road.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, and that is why it is listed as -- identified as one of the objectives to be reached by the special police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On page 2 we further find that after the second stage goals have been completed forces need to be ready to pursue further combat. However, this further combat activity is not defined once the goals of the second stage have been reached, at least not in this order. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The further objectives that have to be reached or fulfilled are not identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can see, Mr. Theunens, that this order was sent for information to the commanders of the Split and Gospic military districts and that this order for combat and use of the special forces of the Ministry of the Interior was approved by deputy minister, signed on the left-hand side, Mr. Zeljko Tomljenovic. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the signature, but I have no reason to doubt about what you're saying, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. The name was not typed, but take my word for it when I say that this is Mr. Tomljenovic's signature, who was the deputy minister to the Minister of the Interior. The use of the special forces of the MUP in combat, as we have seen in several documents by now, can only be done with the approval of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is also what the Law on Internal Affairs states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would ask Mr. Registrar to pull up the document 65 ter 2162.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document by the chief of Main Staff, General Cervenko, dated the 30th of July, 1995. He sent it to the commander of the Split Military District. I want to refer to item 4 of the order. It is ordered that the forces active on the slopes of Mount Velebit -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... translation of count 4. It should be on the second page. Right. [Interpretation] Item 4: "Provide the forces engaged on the slopes of Velebit a special artillery group that will provide them with artillery support." They were supposed to provide support to those forces and the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you quoted, "the MUP forces" went missing in this, but they are back in play. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So first of all, the chief of Main Staff orders the Split Military District to provide artillery support to the forces on Velebit. Evidently they had in mind the forces of the HV but also the MUP forces that were also active in the area of Velebit. Mr. Theunens, is my interpretation correct in terms of this order if I say that the MUP forces are being provided with artillery support but that artillery support was not being put under command of the MUP forces but, rather, they were supposed to provide support to both forces of the HV and of the MUP? Is my interpretation, therefore, correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct on the basis of this document, and the provision of this support will then require coordination between the supported unit, i.e., the special police units and the artillery unit that is providing the support, that's an artillery unit of the Split Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, thank you for that answer. May this be admitted into the evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1094 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May we pull up 65 ter 392, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was issued by the commander of the OG Zadar, Colonel Mladen Fuzul. It is a daily combat report for the 4th of August, that is the first day of Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the central paragraph of the document. It is the fourth paragraph which reads -- [In English] In Croatian page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reads: "The support in Gracac and in-depth for the special forces of MUP was provided by the 120 -- 130-millimetre guns and 122-millimetre howitzers in the first sector. The fact that the SVLR was late in arrival, as well as its ammunition, weakened that support. At around 1300 hours, the 130-millimetre gun was jammed and repaired around 1800 hours. The 203-millimetre howitzer also broke down at around 4.42 p.m. and is still being repaired." Mr. Theunens, this document indicates that the artillery support provided had weaknesses and shortcomings, given that their pieces jammed and broke down. In the course of your expertise, did you come across any other documents which were indicative of certain problems with artillery support?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have included this document in my report, just to clarify it first, on page 273; however, I have also a section on use of artillery by the special police, and I should actually be more complete and include also in support of the special police, and there, for example, quoting from P614 it -- P614 does not mention that there were problems with the artillery. It actually highlights the importance of the artillery, the use of artillery as well as artillery support.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Mr. Theunens, but this one mention. Could I have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1095, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1095 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And just to clarify, the section on artillery in relation to special police is on English pages 305 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to 307, part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we pull up 65 ter 447, please.

utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I said that I would spend some seven to eight minutes on the last issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC

utterances.text: I will finish the cross-examination with this document for today, Your Honour.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, have you had occasion to see this document? utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, and you have the report for 10.00 in the morning. I have the report for 1800.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. I picked up this document just for one example.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May this document be entered into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be D1096. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.text: D1096 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Mikulicic, thank you. Mr. Theunens, we have to deal with a procedural matter totally unrelated to your testimony. I would like to again instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given already or still to be given, and it suddenly slips into my mind that I might have forgotten to remind you at the beginning today that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, but may I take it that you understood and were fully aware that you were still bound by that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. I will be a bit more cautious in announcing the courtroom. This same courtroom, III, Mr. Theunens. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Theunens out of the courtroom. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly. I know the time is somewhat limited. With regard to our request to reply, the issue here, Judge, is the compliance with Rule 94, and what we got most recently with regard to Lieutenant Colonel Theunens is the real expert report that was due to be filed back in February of 2008. If we go through the chronology, there was a Status Conference in July 6th of 2008 where a request was made by -- excuse me, the 7th, I apologise, of July 2008 where a specific -- 2007, excuse me, where a request was made by Mr. Misetic, way back in 2007, with regard to these specific expert reports. There was a discussion with Mr. Tieger where he said he needed additional time in July of 2007 because he was discussing getting documents, more artillery documents, et cetera. As time -- and in that particular -- in that particular Status Conference before Judge Moloto, Judge Moloto --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if I may interrupt you. Until now is there anything you have not yet addressed in your earlier submissions on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It has to do with the chronology as to what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but is there any new matter? Of course we know that February is before July, et cetera. I'm asking whether there's anything new which I've not yet read in your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Judge, and it is a presentation by the Office of the Prosecutor that an expert report was going to be filed when, in fact, the Prosecutor knew at that juncture that there was going to be another expert report filed. So what we got and what was filed in February or January -- the end of January of 2008 wasn't in fact the expert report that the Office of the Prosecutor ever intended to travel on. If you look at that expert report it -- of the 21 pages that were there, less than one page has to do with this case, less than one page, and we get an expert report in -- just several weeks ago that is the real expert report from Lieutenant Konings that has to do with this. Now, what we're going to get from the Office of the Prosecutor is this argument that, "We didn't have -- we couldn't have filed this expert report under these circumstances because we didn't have the information." Rule 94 requires that the accused be given notice as to what the accused has to meet. Now, any argument that they didn't know that they had to be facing targeting issues, I simply address -- point, Your Honour, to the Prosecution's pre-trial brief at paragraph 31 where the issue of military targets is discussed. Certainly prior to trial the Prosecution knew full well that the targeting of military targets in Knin and other towns was going to be a hotly contested issue, and to say at this juncture in their filing that they had to await the unfolding of the evidence during trial in order to file the real expert report by Colonel Konings is a specious argument. One only need to add to -- further to that by looking at Mr. Tieger's opening statement where, at various passages in his opening statement on the 11th of March of 2008, he talks about the targeting of these various locales. So that was an issue. So if we can take this back, there's requests going back well -- there are requests going back well prior to the actual filing of the expert report requesting this. We were told that this was going to be the expert report. Quite clearly they had intended all along that that was not going to be the expert report. How do we know that? We know that because the expert report was actually filed, was completely vacant with regard information concerning this case, but we also know it from e-mail traffic within the Office of the Prosecutor where shortly after the opening statement, there's correspondence between the Map team and Colonel Konings talking about filing a supplement. And it's only -- we can show that particular e-mail to you, if you so -- do we have it? We can put it on the e-mail -- excuse me, on Sanction and we have hard copies if the Court so wants. If we could scroll down a bit in that. And this is dated the 19th of March, 2008. As I noted before the 11th of March, 2008, was the opening statement by the Prosecution. And if we can go to the second paragraph -- excuse me, second page, Mr. Morriss notes that: "In the meantime, we may wish to send you further material to review, after which you may choose to amend your report." So quite clearly, Mr. President, Your Honours, that very early on in this entire process, the Prosecution gave us an expert report that they never intended to be the final expert report, and the problem here, Judge, is they neither told the Defence nor they told the Chamber that they intended all along to file this final expert report of Lieutenant Colonel Konings that was filed in November of 2008, which as I noted is the real expert report which deals with military targets and targeting information directly -- directly in line with the issues that have been presented in this case. If you look back at the first expert report, the first report filed in January 2008 was nothing more than a primer on artillery. Nothing more of the 21 pages was -- 21 pages of what artillery is used for without any direct relevance to this particular case. The relevance to this particular -- barring a half page. The relevance to this particular case only became paramount when he filed his most recent report in -- well, I guess, within the last several weeks. The bottom line, Judge, is if Rule 94 bis is to mean anything, if in fact as 94 bis (A) says that the Prosecution is required to give a full statement of any expert witness, that has got to be given to the Defence prior to trial so, in all fairness, the accused can meet it. The problem here, Judge, is that the Prosecution never -- didn't do that and never intended to do that under these circumstances. They knew that targeting was in information. They knew that was going to be part of the expert report and they didn't put anything into it until this November 2008 filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to add something briefly to that. Of course we've also filed a motion related to Mr. Konings, but along those lines from our standpoint, it's an evolution of the report according to the proof that's come in through the case, and that's -- how are we supposed to meet that? If the reports are constantly going to be coming throughout the case that are adjusted to the proof that's come into the case, how are we supposed to, then, go back and re-cross-examine other witnesses that have already testified in the case? And what's happened specifically in this case is this expert has been provided a list of hypothetical questions, all of which are questions that were raised and dealt with in the cross-examination of witnesses throughout the trial that have dealt on artillery issues. Now, artillery affects our clients in some small fashion, but it affects our client. And with respect to the addendum to the report, all the addendum to the report does is try to fit the opinions or the testimony -- potential testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Konings to the proof that's already been -- to the evidence that's already been submitted in the case and further adjustments of this report really shifts the burden of proof, as far as we're concerned. And that's all I wanted to add, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just add one thing just as a -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Russo, is there anything you would like to add, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, no, Mr. President. Other than fresh mischaracterisations of the Prosecution's position particularly with respect to the e-mail just presented, I don't think's there's anything that's been said which is not already contained in the motion. So I'll stand on our papers.

utterances.text: Thank you for that. The e-mail exchange which we saw on our screen, the parties both want us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the purposes of -- [Overlapping speakers] Yes, Your Honour. For the purposes of this hearing, we'll introduce that into evidence for the consideration of the Chamber.

utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number D1097. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.text: D1097 is -- is admitted into evidence. It's on a procedural matter.

utterances.text: Just on a procedural matter, Mr. President. I understand from my colleague that that has not been uploaded into e-court at this juncture. But I'm --
